headline: The museum says a former curator sold 1,800 stolen objects; he disputes it
said: Hyperallergic reported on 27 March 2024 that the British Museum told the High Court its former senior curator Peter Higgs sold stolen gems and gold jewellery from the storerooms to more than 45 buyers over about ten years, using pseudonyms and altering object records. The museum said a police search of his home in August 2023 found instructions for altering records and coins it says were stolen, which Higgs denies. The report says the court ordered Higgs to disclose information about the objects and that he intends to dispute the claims.
where: Hyperallergic, on a High Court hearing
response: Higgs was represented by lawyers at the March 2024 hearing and, per Hyperallergic, intends to dispute the claims; he denies that the coins found at his home were stolen. No later public statement from him found.
outcome: The court ordered Higgs to disclose information about the objects. The museum says it has recovered about 356 of the missing objects. Former director Hartwig Fischer resigned in August 2023 saying the museum had not responded as it should have to warnings in 2021. No final judgment found.

headline: Protesters and the Tate director say the £50m BP deal has lost public consent
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 20 October 2025 that a protester went on stage during chair George Osborne's speech at the museum's Pink Ball on 18 October with a sign reading "DROP BP NOW", calling the 2023 £50m, ten-year BP sponsorship "cultural cover for a company that is causing climate collapse". Museums Journal reported on 23 October 2025 that Climate Resistance and Energy Embargo for Palestine occupied the Great Court before the ball and that Greece's culture minister called holding a dinner among the Parthenon sculptures offensive to cultural heritage. Museums Journal had reported on 7 June 2024 that Tate director Maria Balshaw told the Observer the public now considers the BP deal inappropriate and that incoming director Nicholas Cullinan would have to deal with "a lot of public dismay".
response: A museum spokesperson told The Art Newspaper in October 2025 that "people are entitled to their views" and that peaceful protest is allowed on site as long as there is no risk to the collection, staff or visitors; Osborne said on the night that "it is great to live in a democracy". In 2024 the museum said the partnership would help maintain public access for generations to come.
outcome: The ball raised £2.5m gross. The BP deal remains in place as of November 2026; the Science Museum's separate BP deal ended in August 2026.

headline: 200 artists say the museum is erasing 'Palestine' from labels; it says not true
said: Hyperallergic reported on 12 March 2026 that an open letter signed by more than 200 artists and cultural groups, including Brian Eno, accused the museum of altering Middle East gallery labels after pressure from UK Lawyers for Israel, calling it part of a "broader erasure of Palestine", and demanded an expert review of the labels and an apology for hosting a private Israeli embassy event in May 2025. The Art Newspaper reported on 19 March 2026 that museum sources said the Ancient Levant labels were revised in early 2025, before UKLFI wrote to the director on 6 February 2026, and that a February 2026 reply from the museum's head of strategy communications said audience testing showed the historic use of the term Palestine was in some circumstances "no longer meaningful". The Art Newspaper had reported on 2 June 2025 that current and former staff were angry about the embassy event and that an internal petition to the director and trustees calling for the museum to cut ties with Israeli cultural institutions had 250 signatures.
where: Open letter reported by Hyperallergic; The Art Newspaper
response: The museum told The Art Newspaper on 3 March 2026: "It is simply not true. We continue to use Palestine across a series of galleries, both contemporary and historic." It told Hyperallergic that some labels and maps had been amended "to show ancient cultural regions". On the May 2025 embassy event it said in June 2025 that "all decisions about commercial events are taken on a non-political basis".

headline: Striking staff say they face in-work poverty while directors earn up to £320,000
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 13 November 2025 that more than 150 PCS members at Tate Britain, Tate Modern, Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives would strike from 26 November to 2 December after rejecting a 3% offer, and that a July 2025 union survey found low morale, rising workloads and members struggling to pay bills; the union said a second restructure in under five years should "raise serious alarm bells" about senior leadership. Novara Media reported on 23 December 2025 that Tate's highest-paid directors received £195,000 to £320,000 in 2024 and that one director's bonus of more than £28,000 exceeded some staff salaries; a curator and PCS rep said staff had been "deprioritised" for years and some used food banks.
where: The Art Newspaper; Novara Media; PCS
response: Tate told The Art Newspaper in November 2025 that it had made savings to fund a 3% rise for most roles, that directors were taking a 0% increase, that two of its three unions had accepted the offer, and that a sustainable financial model was needed "in order to invest in our staff in the long term".
outcome: PCS said in early 2026 that members voted to end the campaign and suspend February strikes after Tate raised the award to 3.6%, restored subsidised hot meals in canteens and agreed a new collective bargaining agreement; the union said the deal still fell short.

headline: Staff call the director's exit 'accountability' for a Tate in 'existential crisis'
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 12 December 2025 that Maria Balshaw, Tate director since 2017, would step down in spring 2026, against a backdrop of a 7% workforce cut, a deficit budget and visitor numbers at Tate Modern 25% below 2019. Museums Journal reported on 18 December 2025 that an anonymous Tate worker speaking for strikers said the institution was in a "clear existential crisis", that senior management had relied on the "trusty shield of Covid and Brexit", and that "people are glad to finally see some sort of accountability taken". Novara Media reported on 23 December 2025 that Paula Orrell of the Contemporary Visual Arts Network said the departure "has to be a consequence" of the strike and of a lack of public funding.
where: Museums Journal; The Art Newspaper; Novara Media
response: Balshaw said in Tate's statement of 12 December 2025 that serving as director had been "an absolute privilege" and that "now is the right time" to hand over to a successor; chair Roland Rudd praised her record. Tate told Museums Journal that directors were taking a 0% rise while most staff got 3%, and cited UK visitor numbers at 95% of pre-pandemic levels.
outcome: Balshaw's last project was the Tracey Emin survey at Tate Modern (February to August 2026). A successor was later announced.

headline: Prospect says East Storehouse staff work 'Amazon-style' shifts without breaks
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 30 July 2026 that Prospect members at the V&A East Storehouse voted unanimously to strike, and 83% across the four London sites, after the union said collections access officers running the "order an object" service were not entitled to morning or afternoon breaks, making it hard to drink water or use the toilet, which it described as Amazon-style conditions; it also cited heatwave working and pay. Museums Journal reported on 6 October 2026 that PCS and Prospect members had walked out for four days in September.
response: The V&A told The Art Newspaper in July 2026 that "all our staff have access to water and toilet facilities and regular breaks while at work", that there are water fountains on every Storehouse floor, and that it pays at least the London Living Wage. In October 2026 it said heatwave measures had included extra breaks, rotations and closing six galleries on the hottest days.
outcome: A half-term strike planned for 29-30 October 2026 was suspended after the V&A offered an average 4.18% rise, 6.9% for the lowest paid, time-and-a-half bank holidays and subsidised food; Acas talks were starting and PCS said it kept its strike mandate.

headline: Staff say the exit scheme and Academy cuts 'feel punitive' while reserves sit at £72m
said: Museums Journal reported on 6 October 2026 that the V&A announced a museum-wide voluntary exit scheme the day before a strike, that PCS said the museum cited a projected £19m cumulative deficit by 2030 while holding £72m in reserves, and that an anonymous staff member said the timing "feels punitive" and that "we just can't see where else they could possibly cut from". The Art Newspaper reported on 26 October 2026 that staff were told on 5 October of plans to dismantle much of the V&A Academy, cutting around half its staff and ending its flagship ten-week courses, even though Academy sales rose more than 22% to £1.2m in 2024-25; unnamed staff said "nobody had any inkling" and that the museum was "full of people who are feeling very demoralised", and senior staff elsewhere had reportedly been asked to find 10-15% cuts.
response: The V&A told Museums Journal in October 2026 that the scheme is "entirely voluntary" and that the £72m reserves were "intentionally built up" and "are not general funds available for day-to-day spending". It told The Art Newspaper on 26 October 2026: "We are still in the consultation phase, and no final decisions have been made", and that it would continue an adult learning programme.
outcome: Consultation on the Academy proposals was due to close on 26 October 2026.

headline: A curator says outsourced security staff are kept apart 'like second-class citizens'
said: HR Grapevine reported on 5 August 2026, citing the Guardian, that a senior curator said the gallery's outsourced CIS Security staff, predominantly from minority ethnic backgrounds, are denied access to the staff hub and subsidised canteen used by directly employed staff and must take breaks in a poorly ventilated basement with rodent problems, which the article called a two-tier workforce. A PCS official wrote in Tribune on 6 March 2026 that the arrangement amounts to indirect discrimination, that CIS had not passed on fully backdated London Living Wage payments, and that some security officers rely on food banks and overdrafts; an anonymous PCS member said: "I sometimes find myself wondering whether I truly belong in this gallery."
response: The National Gallery rejected any link between the separation and ethnicity and attributed the arrangement to space constraints; per Tribune it suggested the employee-only Sunflower café as an alternative.

headline: 200 arts figures say the arts head's removal is 'not an ordinary HR issue'
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 17 February 2026 that Devyani Saltzman, the Barbican's director for arts and participation, would leave in May 2026 after about 18 months, that The Stage reported she had been made redundant, and that Saltzman said the departure was "due to an organisational restructure" and her role would not be replaced. The Art Newspaper reported on 20 February 2026 that an open letter signed by more than 200 people, including John Akomfrah, Jasleen Kaur, Isaac Julien, Salman Rushdie and former Barbican artistic director Graham Sheffield, expressed "profound disappointment and alarm", called the Barbican's framing of the exit as a private staffing matter "inadequate and dismissive" given that Saltzman is one of few leaders of South Asian heritage in its history, and asked the board and the City of London Corporation for a public explanation and an independent review of senior appointments and exits.
where: Open letter reported by The Art Newspaper
response: The Barbican first told The Art Newspaper it was "unable to comment on individual staffing matters", then issued a statement in February 2026 saying Saltzman would leave after "two highly successful years" following "a phase of artistic and organisational transition" ahead of the building's closure for renewal in 2028. Asked about the letter, it referred the paper to that statement.

headline: Lenders and artists pull works from Unravel, calling a cancelled Gaza talk censorship
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 8 March 2024 that after the Barbican cancelled a London Review of Books lecture by Pankaj Mishra on Gaza and the Holocaust, collectors Lorenzo Legarda Leviste and Fahad Mayet withdrew two Loretta Pettway quilts from the gallery's Unravel exhibition on 29 February, accusing the centre of "censorship and repression", and the artists Yto Barrada and Cian Dayrit then asked for their works to be removed. Barrada wrote that it was hard to take seriously "a public institution that does not hold a space for free thinking and debate".
response: Chief executive Claire Spencer said in March 2024 that the Barbican regretted it could not arrange the logistics to host the LRB series, was reviewing how the decision was made, "should have done better", and apologised to artists, lenders and curators. The gallery removed the works, installed signage explaining their absence and said the show would not close early.
outcome: The Art Newspaper reported in September 2024 that the Barbican would host a Palestinian literature festival.

headline: 182 staff demand the opera director answer for snatching a flag on stage
said: The National reported on 6 August 2025 that more than 182 RBO dancers, singers, musicians and staff signed an open letter to chief executive Alex Beard and the board asking that opera director Oliver Mears be "held accountable for his public display of aggression" after he tried to take a Palestinian flag from performer Daniel Perry at an Il Trovatore curtain call on 19 July 2025, and that the RBO stop supplying productions to the Israeli Opera; Perry told The Times that Mears said he would be banned from performing there again. Novara Media reported on 5 August 2025 that the RBO told staff a 2026 Tel Aviv Tosca directed by Mears was cancelled, that staff called it a "win", and that Perry called it a "step in the right direction" that could also be a way to "distract us".
where: Staff open letter reported by The National and Novara Media
response: Alex Beard told the Guardian that the events of 19 July "were without precedent", that the RBO had "reviewed our internal protocols" and wants its stage "free from individual political statements", and that he and the board respect the range of views held by staff, artists and audiences. No public reply from Oliver Mears found.
outcome: The Tel Aviv Tosca was cancelled in August 2025; per Novara, management had not addressed the letter's four demands.

headline: Staff vote no confidence in leadership over a second round of mass redundancies
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 27 February 2025 that the Royal Academy planned to cut up to 60 roles, about 18% of its workforce, forecasting a £7.1m loss for 2024-25, and that an IWGB representative blamed "reckless mismanagement of an historic institution". It reported on 17 March 2025 that around 50 IWGB members protested at the RA, that the union put the jobs at risk at almost 100, and that in a union-run vote 78% of 118 participating staff said they had no confidence in the president, interim chief executive and treasurer to lead the restructure.
response: An RA spokesperson denied the union's figure in March 2025, saying "no decisions have been taken and this is subject to consultation" and that nearly half the 60 roles were vacant. Interim chief executive Natasha Mitchell said the RA faced "a serious financial challenge", had a "robust plan" and understood "the profound impact these proposed changes will have".
outcome: Simon Wallis was appointed chief executive in June 2025.

headline: Former staff say redundancies hit everyone warned over a pro-Palestine letter
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 5 July 2024 that a statement from Cultural Workers Against Genocide said 14 ICA staff were told on 13 March 2024 their roles would be made redundant, and that every staff member who had received an informal warning in October 2023 over an Israel-boycott letter posted on the ICA website without management approval was among them. One former worker, speaking anonymously, said the financial explanation was "a smokescreen" and that a private donor who withdrew over the war had given an amount that was "not significant".
where: Cultural Workers Against Genocide statement reported by The Art Newspaper
response: Director Bengi Ünsal said in July 2024 that after years of operating deficits the ICA "were left with no option other than to restructure the organisation, which sadly involved redundancies"; a spokesperson declined to comment on the donor claim. In January 2025 the ICA called claims that staff were made redundant for pro-Palestinian activism "categorically untrue".

headline: New Contemporaries artists walk out of their own opening over Bloomberg money
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 16 January 2025 that more than 20 artists in the New Contemporaries exhibition walked out of its preview on 14 January to join Gaza Biennale and Palestinian Youth Movement protesters calling on the ICA to cut ties with sponsor Bloomberg Philanthropies, and that artist Fi Isidore said 28 artists had co-written a solidarity statement before leaving. Protesters projected Gaza Biennale works onto the ICA's walls.
response: The ICA said the protest was "misguided" and based on misinformation, that it had received no Bloomberg funding since 2020 and that any funding went directly to New Contemporaries. New Contemporaries confirmed an undisclosed sum from Bloomberg Philanthropies and said it was "fully supportive of the artists' right to protest".

headline: A teachers' union urges schools to boycott the museum over Adani and BP sponsorship
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 10 June 2025 that the National Education Union backed a schools boycott of the Science Museum over its deals with BP and Adani Green Energy, a subsidiary of a group with weapons-manufacturing ties, with a union representative saying helping those companies "pull the wool over our eyes is not contributing to our children's education"; four London schools reportedly agreed not to send trips on the campaign's first day. The Art Newspaper reported on 31 August 2026 that Chris Garrard of Culture Unstained said the museum had "finally come to its senses" when the BP deal ended, criticised the director for championing the partnership "year after year", and called it a "partial victory" because the Adani deal continues.
response: A Science Museum Group spokesperson said in June 2025 it was "proud to deliver free and inspirational experiences to hundreds of thousands of school children every year" and that the Adani-sponsored Energy Revolution gallery had drawn over half a million visitors. In August 2026 it said the BP partnership ended "at the end of its agreed term" and that reports of a ten-year deal to 2028 were inaccurate.
outcome: The BP sponsorship ended on 31 August 2026 after about 25 years. The Adani Green Energy sponsorship continues.

headline: The space closes two years after 25 artists 'deauthored' works over Israel links
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 30 November 2023 that Anita and Poju Zabludowicz would close their Chalk Farm space on 17 December 2023 after 16 years and "significantly" reduce staff, and that in 2021 the group Boycott/Divest Zabludowicz had led 25 artists to disaffiliate from their works in the collection over the couple's links with Israel. Artnet News reported that BDZ alleged Poju Zabludowicz's investment group Tamares was "initially established with money historically made from arms dealing and contracts with the Israeli Air Force" and cited property ties to the West Bank settlement Ma'ale Adumim.
response: A collection spokesperson told Artnet News in late 2023 that "the closure has no connection to the Gaza / Israel war, or any boycott". The couple's website says Tamares has no West Bank investments or military-related interests and that they consider West Bank settlements "unethical and a violation of international law".
outcome: The London space closed on 17 December 2023; the Finnish residency and New York space continued.

headline: The gallery is accused of nepotism for giving a major donor a solo show
said: ArtReview reported on 23 January 2025 that the gallery faced accusations of nepotism over Legends, an exhibition of portraits by Zoë Law, whose Law Family Charitable Foundation the Guardian reported was a major donor to the gallery's £40m redevelopment, and that the gallery had also acquired Law's portrait of Noel Gallagher for its collection. ArtReview amended the article after the gallery complained that an earlier version wrongly said the ethics committee had not been made aware of the decision to exhibit Law's work.
response: The gallery told ArtReview in January 2025 that it "followed our processes", that its grants and donations policy ensures due diligence, and that its ethics committee "were consulted and agreed the donation from The Law Family Charitable Foundation".

headline: Union says the 2025 layoffs were done without notice or representation
said: UAW Local 2110 says the Guggenheim laid off 20 employees, 14 of them union members, on 28 February 2025 without advance notice and without union representation in the meetings where they were told, and that the museum refused to release the names of those cut; the union filed a grievance and a complaint with the National Labor Relations Board. The Art Newspaper reported on 28 February 2025 that curators and executives were not affected and that senior leaders would not take pay cuts. At a rally outside the Rashid Johnson opening on 16 April 2025, reported by Hyperallergic, a laid-off archives worker of more than 30 years said she could have been reassigned or had her salary reduced instead of being cut without notice.
response: A museum spokesperson told Hyperallergic in April 2025 that finances required reducing staff and reorganising teams, and that "all terms of our contract negotiated with UAW Local 2110 have been adhered to". Director Mariët Westermann wrote to staff, as quoted by The New York Times via The Art Newspaper, that the museum's "overall financial picture is not where it needs to be".
outcome: Hyperallergic reported on 2 October 2026 that the Guggenheim union ratified a second contract.

headline: Guggenheim staff vote 93% to authorise a strike over pay and healthcare
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 30 June 2026 that 93% of unionised Guggenheim workers voted to authorise a strike after six months of talks on a second contract, the first having expired in December 2025. The union said entry-level pay was $49,920 and about half of staff earned under $71,000, the level the city says a single adult needs; its chair said workers took the brunt of the 2025 cuts while leadership "did not give up a penny in their salaries". The union asked for 5% then 4.25% raises over three years; the museum offered 3% then 2.75% a year over four.
response: A Guggenheim spokesperson told The Art Newspaper on 30 June 2026 that the museum was negotiating "in good faith", that its "priority remains reaching a fair and economically sustainable agreement", and that the two sides had already agreed on several issues.
outcome: Hyperallergic reported on 2 October 2026 that the Guggenheim union ratified its second contract without setting a strike deadline.

headline: Leadership reshuffle before Abu Dhabi opening lands amid layoffs and stalled talks
said: Hyperallergic reported on 9 April 2026 that Mariët Westermann was restructuring the Guggenheim's leadership before the Abu Dhabi outpost opens, hiring the Hirshhorn's Melissa Chiu to run the Manhattan museum from 1 September 2026 while Westermann oversees the international branches. Hyperallergic described the museum as facing an extended period of fiscal instability, three rounds of controversial layoffs in six years, union anger over the 2025 cuts, and a Gulf Labor Coalition call to boycott the Abu Dhabi project. The Art Newspaper reported the same day that Chiu would work under Westermann.
response: Westermann said in the announcement quoted by both outlets that Chiu has "an outstanding and inspiring track record of leadership in the arts". No reply on the finances or the boycott call was found in either report.
outcome: Chiu started as director on 1 September 2026, per the appointment reports.

headline: Whitney union sets a strike for Lichtenstein preview week, settles the night before
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 29 September 2026 that UAW Local 2110 members at the Whitney, who had voted in mid-September to authorise a strike, set an open-ended strike for 5 October, the week of press previews for the Roy Lichtenstein retrospective. The union said pay was inadequate for New York's cost of living, healthcare costs were rising, and the museum's endowment of over $1bn and executive pay showed it could afford a $71,000 floor. Earlier, on 27 May 2026, the paper reported union members handing out flyers at the 19 May gala behind police barricades that organisers called antagonistic.
response: A Whitney spokesperson told The Art Newspaper on 29 September 2026 that the museum "continues bargaining in good faith" and is committed to a fair contract; in May a spokesperson said it was "committed to arriving at a fair, reasonable contract that respects the needs of all parties".
outcome: Hyperallergic reported on 5 October 2026 that the union ratified a contract on the night of 4 October with raises of at least 14.75%, a $26 an hour floor for visitor, membership and retail staff, longevity bonuses and 12 weeks of paid parental leave.

headline: Unions say the 2025 layoffs breached contracts while the director earned over $1m
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 12 and 26 February 2025 that the Brooklyn Museum planned to cut 47 staff, about 10% of its workforce, citing a deficit approaching $10m. DC 37 Local 1502 and UAW Local 2110 said they were not consulted, that the plan may breach their contracts, that leadership was not bargaining in good faith and had spent lavishly despite knowing cuts might be needed; they sent a cease-and-desist letter. The paper noted that director Anne Pasternak's salary exceeded $1m in 2023 according to public filings, and that senior leaders would take pay cuts of up to 20%. DC 37's executive director told a City Council hearing on 28 February 2025 that no one should lose their job "until we exhaust everything possible".
response: Pasternak told staff by email, quoted by The Art Newspaper on 12 February 2025, that the museum was "experiencing strong headwinds" from inflation and slow attendance recovery. A spokesperson said on 26 February 2025 that the museum respects employees' right to organise and rally and remained in active negotiations under the contracts.
outcome: Hyperallergic reported on 24 March 2025 that the museum paused the layoffs after the city confirmed extra funding and 27 unionised workers accepted buyouts; at least five non-union staff had already received notices. Hyperallergic reported on 2 October 2026 that the museum's union ratified a second contract.

headline: Activists tag leaders' homes over 'complicity'; museum and AAMD call it antisemitic
said: Hyperallergic reported on 12 June 2024 that the homes of director Anne Pasternak, the board chair, the board treasurer and the president and COO were painted with red triangles and slogans, and that an anonymous group claimed responsibility, saying it was answering the museum's "shameless complicity in genocide" and the heavily policed pro-Palestine protest of 31 May 2024 at which dozens were arrested. The group also criticised the treasurer's ties to the investment firm Blackstone and accused the museum of working with the NYPD. The NYPD said it was investigating as a hate crime.
response: A museum spokesperson told Hyperallergic on 12 June 2024 that the museum was "deeply troubled by these horrible acts"; the museum had earlier said the police response on 31 May was devastating but that it had not called the police. The Association of Art Museum Directors condemned the action as antisemitic. Hyperallergic said it had contacted the treasurer and Blackstone and reported no reply.
outcome: No arrests or charges were reported in the article.

headline: Protesters name five trustees over arms investments; 33 staff sign ceasefire letter
said: Hyperallergic reported on 10 February 2024 that more than 500 pro-Palestinian protesters occupied MoMA's atrium and handed out imitation pamphlets naming trustees Leon Black, Larry Fink, Paula Crown, Marie-Josée Kravis and Ronald S. Lauder, alleging investments in Israeli weaponry and surveillance; the museum closed for the rest of the day. The Art Newspaper reported on 14 February 2024 that more than 30 current MoMA employees, with 175 others, signed an open letter accusing leadership of "profound silence" on Gaza and calling for a ceasefire. Earlier, in 2021, the Strike MoMA campaign targeted trustees over ties to Jeffrey Epstein, private prisons and Puerto Rican debt, as Hyperallergic and Artnet reported.
response: No reply from MoMA or the named trustees to the February 2024 pamphlets or the staff letter was found in either report; Hyperallergic said MoMA had not responded to its request for comment. In 2021 MoMA spokespeople said protesters "chose not to act safely or peacefully", per Artnet.

headline: Lowry's exit after 30 years read against union fights, trustee rows and a leaked email
said: Hyperallergic reported on 10 September 2024 that Glenn Lowry would step down in 2025 and set the announcement against staff pickets and walkouts during stalled union talks, a 2022 offer of job security in exchange for two years without raises, and the 2021 Strike MoMA campaign calling him "gaslighter-in-chief" after a leaked email in which he denied that security attacked protesters. The piece also noted climate protests over chair Marie-Josée Kravis's family firm's fossil-fuel investments. The Art Newspaper reported on 28 March 2025 that the board unanimously chose chief curator Christophe Cherix as successor and that Leon Black, who stepped back as chair amid scrutiny of his Epstein ties, still sits on the board.
response: In the 2021 email quoted by Hyperallergic, Lowry wrote that "at no time did a security officer attack a protester". On the succession, Kravis praised Cherix's "steady stewardship" and Lowry called him a gifted curator, per The Art Newspaper on 28 March 2025.
outcome: Cherix took over as director in September 2025, per The Art Newspaper.

headline: Workers rally with a billboard telling director Connie Butler to settle a fair contract
said: Hyperallergic reported on 26 February 2024 that about 75 people rallied outside MoMA PS1 on 23 February with a truck-mounted billboard showing director Connie Butler and the message "Director Butler: Support your employees and settle a fair contract now!". IUOE Local 30 said its contract had expired in November 2023, that some maintenance workers earned as little as $19.50 an hour, that leadership claimed the economic outlook left no room for raises while restoring managerial posts and upgrading equipment, and that Butler had not attended any bargaining session.
response: A PS1 spokesperson told Hyperallergic the museum is "committed to reaching a new contract with Local 30", and its director of external affairs called the process productive. No reply from Butler was found.

institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (The Met)
headline: Met staff vote 76% to unionise after four years, citing job security and transparency
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 19 January 2026 that Met staff from more than 50 departments voted 542 to 172 to join UAW Local 2110 after nearly four years of organising, with 100 ballots challenged by the museum. Organisers said the drive was driven by concerns about job security, pay and transparency around employment policies; a conservator of 16 years said staff do not have to accept whatever they are offered.
response: A Met spokesperson told The Art Newspaper that leadership looks forward to engaging with the UAW, that the museum offers salaries and benefits exceeding industry standards, that over 600 employees earn more than $100,000 a year, and that salaries have risen 4% over five years.
outcome: The challenged ballots were to be resolved through an NLRB-overseen arbitration both sides agreed to, per the report.

institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (The Met)
headline: DA's seizures from the Met pass $95m; condition reports cited as evidence of looting
said: Hyperallergic reported on 1 July 2026, following The New York Times, that objects worth about $95m have been surrendered by the Met to the Manhattan District Attorney's Antiquities Trafficking Unit since 2017, 120 of them individually valued, with a further batch removed in June 2026 including pieces acquired between 1971 and 2001 from Italy, Greece, Egypt and Turkey. Investigators said the museum's own condition reports noting objects arriving encrusted in dirt had served as evidence of illegal digging. In 2022 Hyperallergic reported, from search warrants, that 23 looted antiquities were seized from the home of Met trustee Shelby White.
response: The Met told Hyperallergic the objects were not seized but sent to the DA after being flagged by its own 12-person provenance team, led since 2023 by Lucian Simmons, who said assessments are "neither straightforward nor speedy"; it said it has made 18 restitutions on its own since 2017. In 2022 the Met declined to comment on the White seizure and White could not be reached.
outcome: Objects have been restituted to Greece and Turkey in April and June 2026, per Hyperallergic.

headline: Staff fired over keffiyehs; protesters call for Amy Hau to go; Lahiri refuses award
said: The Art Newspaper and Hyperallergic reported in September 2024 that the Noguchi Museum fired three gallery attendants for wearing keffiyehs under a dress code revised in August 2024 to ban political dress, after more than 50 of 72 staff signed a petition against the policy and 14 walked out on 21 August. At a rally on 8 September 2024 protesters called on director Amy Hau to step down; one fired worker called the ban "the stupidity and the irony of a cultural institution banning a cultural garment". Hyperallergic reported on 26 September 2024 that Jhumpa Lahiri declined the museum's 2024 Isamu Noguchi Award over the policy.
response: The museum said the decisions concerned personnel matters it could not discuss, that such expressions "can unintentionally alienate segments of our diverse visitorship", and that it had decided to remove political statements from the workplace. Hau said in a posted message, per Hyperallergic, that the museum was not founded as an advocacy organisation and cannot speak for Isamu Noguchi. On Lahiri, a spokesperson said "We respect her perspective".
outcome: Staff voted unanimously in January 2025 to join UAW Local 2110, per Hyperallergic; anonymous activists placed mock wall labels in the galleries in December 2024, per The Art Newspaper.

headline: Union formed after the keffiyeh firings; workers vote to authorise a strike in 2026
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 19 December 2024 that Noguchi staff petitioned for a union with UAW Local 2110 citing a need for "greater transparency" and "better conditions", with the keffiyeh dismissals as the focal point of wider dissatisfaction. Hyperallergic reported on 15 January 2025 that the vote was unanimous and the unit covers about 55 of 72 employees. The Art Newspaper reported on 29 September 2026 that Noguchi workers had voted to authorise a strike while bargaining with the museum.
response: The museum said in January 2025, per Hyperallergic, that it "acknowledges and respects our staff's decision to unionize" and looks forward to working constructively with Local 2110. No reply on the 2026 strike authorisation was found.

headline: Tallant leaves for the Hayward after staff rows over Gaza, surveillance and an OBE
said: Hyperallergic reported on 21 January 2026 that Sally Tallant would leave the Queens Museum in summer 2026 to run the Hayward Gallery in London, and recalled that in November 2023 staff asked leadership to address Gaza and she said the museum could not make political statements, and that a coalition of anonymous artists in a 2023 report accused her of dismissing concerns about the Year of Uncertainty residency, fostering a climate of fear and accepting a British OBE while running a museum in a very diverse borough. Hyperallergic reported on 17 November 2023 that anonymous staff described "heightened surveillance", one-on-one meetings and new work phones after their letter, and that Tallant had emailed that circulating it by museum email breached harassment and solicitation policies.
response: In a recorded November 2023 staff meeting quoted by Hyperallergic, Tallant said the museum "is not able to make political statements", citing its nonprofit status, bylaws and the AAM Code of Ethics. The museum had not replied to Hyperallergic's request for comment in 2023. On her departure the museum praised her record of more than 30 exhibitions.
outcome: The board began a search for a new president and executive director in January 2026.

headline: Phillips retires after 26 years marked by labour disputes and a $900k pay gap
said: Hyperallergic reported on 25 September 2025 that Lisa Phillips would step down in April 2026 when her contract ends, as the $82m expansion completes, and set this against repeated disputes in which unionised staff accused management of poor conditions, unfair labour practices and stalled talks, and questioned the gap between staff pay and her compensation of nearly $900,000 in 2024 tax filings. The union, part of UAW Local 2110, had filed an NLRB complaint alleging the 18 pandemic-era layoffs in 2020 targeted union supporters.
response: Phillips said the reopening "presents the ideal moment to pass the baton to a new generation of leaders", per The Art Newspaper on 26 September 2025. On the 2020 NLRB charge the museum said it did not believe the claim had merit, per Hyperallergic. The union said it looks forward to a good bargaining relationship with new leadership.
outcome: Phillips becomes director emeritus and will curate a Bowery exhibition; the search for a successor began in September 2025.

headline: Workers picket the gala over $19 an hour pay and two years without a first contract
said: Hyperallergic reported on 7 May 2026 that about three dozen AFAM workers and UAW Local 2110 organisers picketed the museum's gala at the Mandarin Oriental on 6 May, saying frontline staff earn $19 an hour, that talks on a first contract had stalled for nearly two years since the June 2024 union vote, that the museum offered $21.50 against a request of $30 by year three without guaranteeing existing benefits, and that unionised positions were cut and outsourced during the 2025 renovation closure. The union called the bargaining "bad-faith" and noted the CEO's 2024 compensation of $321,882 from tax filings.
response: A museum spokesperson told Hyperallergic on 7 May 2026 that the museum respects employees' decision to unionise and is committed to good-faith bargaining toward a fair, mutually beneficial contract.
outcome: Hyperallergic reported a tentative agreement on 29 September 2026 and ratification of the first contract on 2 October 2026.

headline: Faculty union says SVA's quiet layoffs of about 30 put the budget burden on workers
said: Hyperallergic reported on 15 August 2025 that SVA president David Rhodes announced staff cuts in a brief all-staff email on 5 August citing "financial challenges", and that the newly formed faculty union, SVA Faculty United - UAW, estimated about 30 layoffs across the library, programmes and support staff, with courses cancelled over low enrolment, which fell to 3,812 in 2024 from 4,016. A union organiser said the administration was placing the burden on its workers. The Art Newspaper reported the same on 22 August 2025. In an April 2025 opinion piece in Hyperallergic, an adjunct wrote that SVA was one of the last New York schools without a faculty union and lagged peers on pay and benefits.
response: Rhodes wrote in the 5 August 2025 email that affected employees had been notified and were receiving support. Hyperallergic said SVA did not respond to multiple requests to confirm the numbers or comment on the cancelled classes.

headline: Investigation says the museum holds 12,000 human remains and kept descendants in the dark
said: Hyperallergic reported on 16 October 2023 on an investigation by John Jay College professor Erin L. Thompson, drawing on annual reports and nearly a dozen anonymous current and former staff, saying the museum holds about 12,000 human remains, including 2,200 Native Americans, dozens of Black New Yorkers from 1940s medical schools, five people believed to have been enslaved taken from an Inwood burial ground, and about 500 bodies from a 1939–41 expedition at Point Hope, Alaska, whose elders did not know the remains were in New York. Thompson argued the catalogue is not public and that unclaimed remains do not justify withholding them.
response: President Sean M. Decatur emailed staff the week before publication announcing that the museum would remove human remains from display, and said in a statement to Hyperallergic that the enslaved individuals' treatment deprived them of "basic human dignity"; the museum said it adopted repatriation procedures and plans new storage.
outcome: The museum announced it would stop displaying human remains from its collection, per the report.

headline: Unions say the jewel heist was a predictable catastrophe they had warned about
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 20 October 2025, the day after the theft of crown jewels from the Galerie d'Apollon, that Elise Muller of the union SUD Culture called it "a predictable catastrophe" and said staff had raised the alarm over "severe failings" while attention and money went to gala dinners, concerts, VIP visits and fashion week. The CGT said 200 posts had been cut since 2010 and the CFDT asked for an independent security audit. The paper also cited a Radio France report on an unpublished Cour des comptes pre-report describing "considerable and persistent" delays in maintaining technical installations, with only about a third of rooms covered by cameras.
response: The museum declined to comment to The Art Newspaper on 20 October 2025. At a Senate hearing on 22 October 2025 president Laurence des Cars acknowledged that the only camera on the wall where the thieves entered faced away from the point of entry and that camera expansion had lagged (The National, 25 February 2026). Culture minister Rachida Dati later cited an administrative investigation finding "a chronic under-estimation" of burglary risks (The Art Newspaper, 8 December 2025).
outcome: A parliamentary inquiry's preliminary report cited "systemic failures"; des Cars resigned on 24 February 2026.

headline: Striking staff say trust with the director is broken and the €666m entrance plan must go
said: A strike notice from CFDT-Culture, SNMD CGT-Culture and SUD Culture Solidaires dated 8 December 2025 says internal alerts "remained a dead letter", that a "pyramidal and compartmentalised" governance produces "absurd decisions", and that Abu Dhabi licence money should go to palace repairs rather than the new entrance. The Art Newspaper reported on 6 January 2026 that 350 staff including curators voted unanimously to strike, that a CFDT representative described "the complete breach of trust between the staff and the director, Laurence des Cars", and that unions call the €666m redevelopment "unrealistic". The paper added that the Cour des comptes had found the entrance project had "no financial viability".
where: CGT-Culture strike notice; The Art Newspaper
response: No formal statement from the museum on the strike was found. Deputy administrator Francis Steinbeck told BFM-TV the poor state of the equipment "was known for years" (The Art Newspaper, 8 December 2025). The museum's 2026 budget set €100m for preliminary studies of the entrance and €15m for technical maintenance.
outcome: Rolling strikes ran from mid-December 2025, the longest in the museum's history; des Cars resigned on 24 February 2026 and the architecture competition for the entrance was suspended (The Art Newspaper, 3 April 2026).

headline: MPs say a 'hyper presidency' accumulated failures before des Cars resigned
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 24 February 2026 that Laurence des Cars resigned after the heist, the longest strikes in the museum's history and a ten-year ticket fraud estimated at €10m, and that members of a parliamentary inquiry committee denounced a "hyper presidency which has accumulated failures"; its chair Alexandre Portier said that elsewhere such a list "would have since long led to the departure of the director". The paper noted that under 3% of the budget had gone to safety since 2021 while the €666m entrance project went ahead. On 3 April 2026 it quoted union representative Elise Muller calling her management "top down, haughty and brittle" and an unnamed curator saying the atmosphere changed "from one day to another" when Christophe Leribault arrived.
response: President Macron called the resignation "an act of responsibility" and asked des Cars to lead a G7 museum-cooperation mission (The Art Newspaper, 24 February 2026). No reply from des Cars to the committee's criticism was found. On the ticket fraud, a museum spokesperson told The Art Newspaper the arrests were part of a plan against "intensifying and diversifying ticket fraud" (16 February 2026).
outcome: Christophe Leribault was named president of the Louvre on 25 February 2026 with a mission Macron described as "appeasement".

headline: Staff say the collection is hired out while they are told nothing about their future
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 8 December 2023 that unions had struck since mid-October, closing the building for eight days, and demanded written guarantees on jobs and no outsourcing ahead of the five-year closure, with a petition passing 2,200 signatures. Artnet, reporting on the unions' letter of 21 November 2023, quoted a curator saying the director was "crisscrossing the planet with three jokers: Henri Matisse, Constantin Brancusi, and Vassily Kandinsky", and the letter warning that "the frantic race for resources sacrifices the fundamental mission of heritage conservation", citing paid loan deals with AlUla, H'ART Amsterdam, La Caixa, SFMOMA and Shanghai.
response: A Pompidou spokesperson told The Art Newspaper that "all employees will be maintained and recover their posts or an equivalent at the reopening"; a source close to the culture minister said it was "absolutely impossible to make such detailed commitments seven years in advance" (8 December 2023). Director Laurent Le Bon defended the plan at a 24 October 2023 press conference as "exceptional, and unique" (Artnet).
outcome: The strike ended with an agreement in December 2023; the building closed in September 2025 until 2030.

headline: Jersey City's mayor says the Pompidou outpost is dead; Brussels' CD&V wants out of Kanal
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 12 February 2026 that Jersey City mayor James Solomon said "We will not be doing Pompidou, to be clear. It is dead", after revealing a $255m city deficit; a 2023 report by a Republican state senator had called the project "a circus of waste and excess". In Brussels, La Libre reported on 20 May 2025 that CD&V group leader Benjamin Dalle said Kanal-Centre Pompidou risked becoming "a monument of financial mismanagement", called the Pompidou collaboration costly and said it "is not set in stone", proposing to end it after the agreement expires at the end of 2027.
response: A Centre Pompidou spokesperson told ARTnews, as quoted by Dezeen on 13 February 2026, that "on September 15, the newly elected mayor Mr James Solomon decided not to pursue this project". No Pompidou reply to the CD&V proposal on Kanal was found.
outcome: The Jersey City project is cancelled; Kanal is due to open on 28 November 2026 with the Pompidou agreement running to the end of 2027.

headline: A patron quits over 'wokeism' and a Palestine show; 180 art figures sign in defence
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 8 May 2024 that collector Sandra Hegedüs resigned from the Amis du Palais de Tokyo after 15 years, writing on Instagram that she did not want "to be associated with the new, very political direction at the Palais de Tokyo", accusing it of "wokeism" and calling the exhibition Past Disquiet "biased and misleading"; the post drew over 13,000 likes. The Art Newspaper France reported on 13 May 2024 that the DCA network of 54 art centres launched a petition and open letter in Le Monde signed by about 180 directors, curators and artists, warning that social-media "tribunals" endanger artists and institutional freedom; the petition shows 9,058 signatures.
response: The Palais de Tokyo said it "strongly rejects the accusations levelled against it on social media", condemned terrorism and antisemitism and called for a Gaza ceasefire and the release of hostages; president Guillaume Désanges said the institution must engage with political questions as "a space for debate, reflection and encounters"; Amis president Philippe Dian said the group exists to support the Palais, not to judge its programming (The Art Newspaper, 8 May 2024).
outcome: Past Disquiet ran to 30 June 2024 as planned.

headline: The press asks why Pinault Collection presidents keep leaving after months in the job
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 27 March 2026 that Guillaume Cerutti was stepping down as president of the Pinault Collection after 13 months, that there had been "no explanation for his departure", and that neither he nor François Pinault would comment. PaintAndPainting wrote on 7 April 2026 that Cerutti's exit followed those of Sylvain Fort after about six months in 2019, Martin Bethenod in 2021 and executive general director Denis Berthomier in June 2025, and suggested that the patriarch, turning 90, "continues to maintain control" and that the tone of Cerutti's LinkedIn farewell "suggests a poorly prepared exit".
response: A Pinault Collection spokesperson confirmed the departure to The Art Newspaper on 26 March 2026 and said there were "no plans to appoint a new president of the organisation or an interim"; Cerutti and François Pinault declined to comment on the reason.
outcome: Emma Lavigne remains director general; no new president has been named.

headline: Le Monde says the foundation is a tax write-off; Arnault calls the series biased
said: USA Art News reported on 28 July 2026 that a six-part Le Monde investigation by Raphaëlle Bacqué and Vanessa Schneider, begun on 19 July, argued that Bernard Arnault's patronage, centred on the Fondation Louis Vuitton, gave LVMH large tax advantages under the 60% and 90% deduction rules and served to project influence and market the brand, calculating that the €43m Caillebotte purchase cost the group €4.3m after deductions. NSS Magazine reported that Le Monde portrayed Arnault as an "art lover obsessed with tax write-offs".
where: Le Monde, as reported by USA Art News and NSS Magazine
response: Arnault published a three-page open letter on LVMH's X account on 26 July 2026 calling the series "biased", saying he funded the foundation under the 2003 patronage law and that if lawmakers object to the system they should change it, and writing "I gave, and that seems suspicious" (USA Art News and NSS Magazine, 28 July 2026).

headline: Scientists say the Grand Palais is squeezing out the Palais de la Découverte
said: Politis reported on 25 June 2025 that the Palais de la Découverte's reopening in the Grand Palais, set for 11 June 2025, was postponed, that the government dismissed Universcience president Bruno Maquart on 12 June, and that a petition "Sauvons le Palais de la découverte" passed 80,000 signatures with signatories including Jean Jouzel and Cédric Villani, while culture minister Rachida Dati left open a move of the science museum to La Villette. PaintAndPainting reported on 20 May 2026 that Universcience chair Sylvie Retailleau said Grand Palais president Didier Fusillier had asked Universcience to help finance the renovation, that a 1,200 m² gallery was sold to the Grand Palais, and that "we didn't come far from not having it at all".
response: Didier Fusillier told The Art Newspaper on 9 July 2025 that the question "does not fall within my remit" and that "some are trying to create the impression that science has suddenly vanished from Paris", noting the chief architect had found the Palais d'Antin spaces unfit for use at reopening.
outcome: An agreement was reached: the Palais de la Découverte stays in the Grand Palais with shared use of the Antin rotunda and a 350 m² gallery lent to the Grand Palais until 30 June 2030; Retailleau said "the subject is now closed" (PaintAndPainting, 20 May 2026).

headline: Jack Lang leaves the IMA under pressure over his Epstein ties
said: Reuters, via Internazionale, reported on 7 February 2026 that Jack Lang resigned as president of the Institut du monde arabe in "a decision taken under pressure over Lang's ties to the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein". The Art Newspaper reported on 17 February 2026 that his name appears 673 times in the Epstein files, that he is the subject of an investigation into those ties, and that police searched his office and apartment on the day of his leaving ceremony.
response: Lang said at his leaving ceremony that "it's alright, I have nothing to hide", that he was "completely innocent" and "knew nothing of Epstein's horrific crimes" (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026).
outcome: Diplomat Anne-Claire Legendre was named to replace him on 17 February 2026.

institution: Paris Musées (Réseau des Musées de la Ville de Paris)
headline: Guides at the city's museums strike, saying their pay has not risen in 17 years
said: The Local reported on 24 June 2025 that guides, lecturers and storytellers at around a dozen Paris museums, including the Petit Palais, Carnavalet, the Musée d'Art moderne, Galliera, Cernuschi and the Catacombes, went on strike over pay and job security, saying "their pay has not increased for 17 years" and that many are on short-term or temporary contracts. The museums stayed open but guided tours may not have run. The report placed the action alongside the Louvre walkout the previous week.
response: No statement from Paris Musées or the City of Paris was found in the report.

headline: The PP wants Segade sacked if the museum cannot inventory its 25,000 works by year end
said: El Debate reported on 16 April 2026 that the joint Congress–Senate committee on the Tribunal de Cuentas approved, 20 votes to 13, a Partido Popular motion asking culture minister Ernest Urtasun to remove Manuel Segade as director if the museum has not produced a complete inventory of its holdings reconciled with its accounts by 31 December 2026; the PP says the museum breaches public accounting rules and that nothing has been known since of donations valued at €1,255,550 in the last audit, in 2021. USA Art News reported on 21 May 2026 that the far right backed the motion, the PSOE abstained, and that the Tribunal de Cuentas had earlier criticised the museum's internal controls.
response: Museum sources told El Debate the Reina Sofía is "immersed in a process of internal regularisation" of inventory, valuation, control and security of works, with a valued inventory being produced under the Plan General de Contabilidad Pública (16 April 2026); the museum has launched a records platform called Artis (USA Art News, 21 May 2026). No reply from Segade or the ministry was found.

headline: Israel's ministry says Jewish visitors were thrown out; a lobby group sues the museum
said: El Independiente reported on 16 February 2026 that three Israeli women, one a Holocaust survivor, were insulted by other visitors while carrying an Israeli flag and expelled by a security guard who, according to Okdiario and the European Jewish Congress, said some visitors were uncomfortable that they were Jewish; Israel's acting ambassador Dana Erlich wrote on X "My flag is not a provocation". The Objective reported on 22 February 2026 that Israel's foreign ministry called the episode a "shame" and that the association ACOM announced legal action against the museum and against director Manuel Segade for breaching the neutrality required of a public body, listing at least thirteen pro-Palestinian actions at the museum since October 2023.
response: The museum ordered "the immediate opening of an independent and transparent internal investigation", declared "zero tolerance for any kind of violence" linked to antisemitism and said it would not stop "until the facts are clarified" (El Independiente, 16 February 2026). Segade told ABC, as quoted by The Objective, that museums attract political activism and that a place that houses Guernica has a status it cannot avoid.

headline: Nineteen outsourced mediators are sacked over a 'monumental error' in the museum's tender
said: El Salto reported on 20 February 2024 that contractor Sedena SL notified an ERE for its 19 cultural-mediation workers after the museum's new tender, priced below the existing contract, was thrown out on 19 January 2024 for what the union SUT called "errores insubsanables" and a "monumental error" by the museum; workers said the removal of the head of education was no answer and asked the museum to admit its mistake and rehire them. elDiario.es reported the same day that director Manuel Segade called the error "very serious" and said "this happens because it is an outsourced service. It should not be."
response: The museum admitted a drafting error in the tender, said it had asked Sedena to use a temporary layoff (ERTE) so staff could be rehired after a new tender, and removed the head of its education area (El Salto, 20 February 2024). Segade said he hoped mediators would "little by little" become part of the museum's real structure (elDiario.es, 20 February 2024).
outcome: After an urgent meeting the company switched the ERE to an ERTE and the museum committed to a new tender within six months (elDiario.es, 21 February 2024).

headline: Outsourced visitor staff strike, saying the Prado told them it was 'not its problem'
said: El Salto reported on 7 December 2023 that more than 80 ticketing, reception and cloakroom workers employed by subcontractor Navalservice SL struck on 15–17 December 2023, called by the union SUT, over schedules of up to 60 hours a week, "abusive" temporary contracts, pay below the museum's own staff and what they call "social dumping"; they said the incoming contractor had underbid the Prado's budget by about €500,000 and that the museum told them the dispute was "not its problem" and did not attend a mediation hearing. Izquierda Diario reported on 15 December 2023 that SUT called the minimum services "de facto a ban on the strike".
response: No statement from the Museo del Prado or the contractors was found in either report; the "not its problem" line is the workers' account.
outcome: The contract passed to a joint venture of Iman Seguridad and Alianzas y Subcontratas on 15 December 2023.

headline: A security union says the Prado's guard tender breaks procurement law
said: El Independiente reported on 20 October 2025 that the Prado's outsourced security contract, covering 104 guards and public-facing posts, was out to tender with four bids and a base budget of €9m, up from €7m for the current contract, and that the private-security federation FTSP-USO Madrid had filed a special appeal with the Tribunal Administrativo Central de Recursos Contractuales arguing that article 145 of the public contracts law "is being violated" and asking for the award criteria to be annulled in favour of "genuine technical criteria" on bidders' capacity.
response: No statement from the Prado on the appeal was found in the report; the appeal has no suspensive effect, so the tender continued.

headline: Auditors find 321 of the baroness's works held without any contract, then returned
said: The Tribunal de Cuentas audit of the Fundación Colección Thyssen-Bornemisza for 2020, endorsed by the Comisión Mixta and published in the BOE on 13 August 2025, says up to 321 works belonging to the foundation's vice-president, Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza, were held in storage at the end of 2020 with no contract covering the deposit, that they were also lent to other institutions in 2020, and that 66 works from her collection, more than 10% of it, were lent in 2020, several for more than six months. ESdiario reported on 27 May 2025, citing museum sources, that the number rose to over 400 works before they were withdrawn after the February 2022 agreement with the government.
where: Tribunal de Cuentas report No. 1.514, published in the BOE
response: The foundation told the auditors the works "have already been returned to their owners", a claim the Tribunal did not verify, and argued that loans from her collection were not subject to the six-month limit because the owners wished otherwise, a reading the Tribunal rejected. No reply from Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza was found.
outcome: The Comisión Mixta recommended that loan durations and numbers strictly follow the statutes and that the artistic advisory council lose the power to extend loans (BOE, 13 August 2025).

headline: Solana accuses the press of bad faith over the museum's decolonial turn
said: El Independiente reported on 24 June 2024 that artistic director Guillermo Solana, presenting the exhibition on colonial memory in the Thyssen collections, accused some media of misreporting the museum's decolonisation process and, asked about reports that the government had dictated the programming, said he did not know whether that came from "ignorance or bad faith, I suppose the latter"; he called a question about a Nazi-looted Pissarro "irrelevant". The Objective had reported on 4 June 2024 that Solana appeared, in the symbolic last place, on the Sumar list for the European elections, the party of the culture minister.
response: Solana said he had worked at the museum for almost twenty years and had never received instructions from any government member about exhibitions, and that "decolonising is not a synonym of restituting" (El Independiente, 24 June 2024).

headline: Board members say they were kept in the dark about the prime minister's brother's seat
said: El Debate reported on 20 April 2024 that, after it revealed the appointment of David Sánchez Pérez-Castejón, brother of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, to the Teatro Real's advisory council, president Gregorio Marañón wrote to the board saying he sat there because he "represents the Diputación de Badajoz", is unpaid, and that the government had not increased its contribution by €7m; the paper says this last claim is untrue and that Marañón later acknowledged receiving the money and spending it on solar panels. It reported that members of the advisory council felt "ignored and deceived" because they had not been told of the appointment.
response: The Teatro Real's letter to its board, signed by Gregorio Marañón, said the advisory council's 34 cultural institutions each name their own representative, that Badajoz's performing-arts office chose him, and that the council meets once a year for two hours (El Debate, 20 April 2024). No reply from David Sánchez Pérez-Castejón was found.

headline: A union and a former programmer say Cineteca censored a film about its own workers
said: El Salto reported on 2 September 2023 that Cineteca Madrid, in Matadero, pulled the screening of Transición, a documentary by Saioa Olga González with testimonies from CNT members at the municipal company Madrid Destino about precarious work, from the Cinezeta cycle. The CNT section said "this time from above they have said no, we consider this censorship"; former Cinezeta programmer Guillermo Hormigo said everything indicated the Cineteca's own management censored the cycle and that the management told him it preferred the consequences of not screening the film to the backlash of showing it.
response: The Cineteca's stated reason, as reported by Europa Press and relayed by El Salto, was "management reasons and artistic criteria"; no direct statement from Madrid Destino was found.

headline: A petition asks Fundación Montemadrid to reverse the sudden closure of the photo lab
said: A change.org petition started on 1 February 2024 by a member of the public opposes what it calls the sudden decision to close La Casa Encendida's photography laboratory, describing it as a 20-year-old affordable space for amateurs and professionals and a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community, and asks the Fundación Montemadrid to reconsider. It gathered 2,056 signatures and is now closed.
response: No reply from La Casa Encendida or the Fundación Montemadrid was found on the petition page.

headline: Senate pulls Oyoun's funding over antisemitism claims its own report did not find
said: Artnet reported on 26 March 2024 that Berlin's Senate culture committee froze Oyoun's funding in December 2023, ending a four-year partnership worth about one million euros a year, after culture senator Joe Chialo described a planned event by the Jüdische Stimme as hidden antisemitism; a Senate-commissioned report, Artnet wrote, found no antisemitic activity identifiable on Oyoun's part. The Jüdische Stimme said in a statement carried by The Left Berlin on 28 December 2023 that the cut was censorship aimed at a BPoC space and that four-year funding through 2025 had already been approved before the row. The Jüdische Allgemeine reported on 24 July 2024 that Berlin's constitutional court found Oyoun's rights had been violated, overturned the higher administrative court's March ruling and sent the case back, while leaving open whether Oyoun is owed further funding.
where: Artnet, Jüdische Allgemeine, The Left Berlin
response: The funding stop followed allegations about a November 2023 event on Oyoun's premises, and Chialo's administration halted payments at the end of 2023 (Jüdische Allgemeine, 24 July 2024). Oyoun's lawyer Myrsini Laaser said after the July 2024 ruling that the rule of law had ultimately prevailed.
outcome: Constitutional court of Berlin remanded the case in July 2024; no final ruling on the funding recorded.

headline: Court bars Tagesspiegel from repeating three claims about Oyoun
said: Artnet reported on 26 March 2024 that a Berlin court granted Oyoun an injunction against the Tagesspiegel over a 20 February 2024 article, barring the paper from repeating three allegations, including a claim that the Senate had favoured Oyoun because of family ties, which the court found baseless, and claims about alleged antisemitic incidents, which it found unfounded. Artnet named Green Party member of parliament Susanna Kahlefeld as the source of the Tagesspiegel's claims. Oyoun's representatives said unsubstantiated or refuted allegations should not fall under journalistic freedom of expression, and co-founder Louna Sbou was quoted saying the rule of law looked to her like a facade.
response: No reply from the Tagesspiegel or from Susanna Kahlefeld found in the sources opened.
outcome: Injunction granted on 25 March 2024, per Artnet.

headline: HKW drops rapper's 7 October concert; PEN Berlin says a chance for dialogue was wasted
said: The Berliner Zeitung reported on 29 September 2025 that HKW cancelled a concert by the rapper Chefket planned for 7 October 2025 within Jan Böhmermann's exhibition, citing objections especially from Jewish circles and not wanting any event on the anniversary of the Hamas attack to cast doubt on the house's opposition to antisemitism; federal culture minister Wolfram Weimer had called the concert a provocation (Berliner Zeitung, 1 October) and said the exhibition gave antisemitism a stage. PEN Berlin, the Berliner Zeitung wrote on 1 October 2025, said HKW had missed a chance to hold a dialogue with the artist and asked Böhmermann why he invited and then disinvited him. Swiss broadcaster SRF reported on 1 October 2025 that critic Tobi Müller saw the T-shirt row as a surface trigger for a campaign by Nius and other Springer titles against HKW's director Bonaventure Soh Bejeng Ndikung.
response: HKW said it takes the objections very seriously, is concerned about rising antisemitism and racist violence, and still wants an open dialogue where many viewpoints are heard (Berliner Zeitung, 29 September 2025). Böhmermann rejected Weimer's claim and said he would personally remove anyone denying Israel's right to exist or the Holocaust from the stage. No statement from Ndikung found in the sources opened.

headline: Incoming HKW director accused of closeness to BDS; he denies it and cites racism
said: The Jüdische Allgemeine reported on 25 October 2022 that Bonaventure Ndikung, shortly before taking over HKW, had been accused of closeness to the BDS movement, pointing to his signing of the Initiative GG 5.3 Weltoffenheit and a 2014 Facebook post about Gaza. Ndikung told dpa he does not support BDS, that the initiative rejects the boycott of Israel and the misuse of antisemitism accusations, that he regretted the 2014 post and that Israel's right to exist was non-negotiable for him. He said he believed he was being scrutinised as one of the first African heads of such an institution in Germany and had faced racism in Germany before. Later coverage of the October 2025 concert row (SRF, 1 October 2025) described a continuing press campaign against him.
response: Ndikung denied supporting BDS and said he does not exclude anyone by origin, religion or citizenship (dpa via Jüdische Allgemeine, 25 October 2022).
outcome: Ndikung took up the post in January 2023.

headline: Nan Goldin uses her opening to accuse Germany of weaponising antisemitism
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 25 November 2024 that Nan Goldin, opening her retrospective at the Neue Nationalgalerie, said the word antisemitism had been weaponised in Germany, called what she saw in Gaza a genocide and said tongues had been gagged by the government, the police and a cultural crackdown; pro-Palestinian chants then drowned out director Klaus Biesenbach's reply. ARTnews reported that culture minister Claudia Roth called the speech unbearably one-sided and the chants an attack on the museum, that Berlin culture senator Joe Chialo accused Goldin of ignoring history, and that Josef Schuster of the Central Council of Jews said whoever invites BDS gets BDS. The Art Newspaper also quoted Hermann Parzinger, president of the foundation that runs the museum, calling the speech intolerable in its one-sidedness.
response: Biesenbach said he disagreed with Goldin on the Middle East but stood for her right to express herself freely, condemned the 7 October attack as terror and expressed empathy for civilians in Gaza and Lebanon. The museum said it explicitly distanced itself from the protesters' statements and was committed to free expression and respectful dialogue; ARTnews noted it posted Biesenbach's statement but not Goldin's speech.
outcome: The show ran as planned.

headline: Artists quit Goldin symposium, which she says the museum arranged behind her back
said: ARTnews reported in November 2024 that Hito Steyerl, then Candice Breitz and Eyal Weizman, withdrew from a symposium the Neue Nationalgalerie had organised alongside Nan Goldin's retrospective after Goldin commented on the Strike Germany Instagram account. Goldin said the symposium, curated by Saba-Nur Cheema and Meron Mendel, was arranged without her knowledge and suggested the museum wanted to show it did not back her politics; she stepped back from speaking at it. ARTnews also wrote that German press coverage before the opening had focused on Goldin's signature on a 2023 Artforum ceasefire letter.
response: Klaus Biesenbach said in a statement that the symposium was planned independently of Goldin, would not address her work, would offer space for debate, and that the museum supported her right to her opinion even where it disagreed (ARTnews).

institution: Julia Stoschek Foundation (Julia Stoschek Collection / JSC Berlin)
headline: Stoschek shuts her Berlin space after ten years, calling it a strategic realignment
said: ArtReview reported on 24 April 2026 that the Julia Stoschek Foundation will close its Berlin venue on Leipziger Straße at the end of October 2026 after 22 exhibitions, describing the move as a strategic realignment towards international projects. The Berliner Zeitung wrote on 25 April 2026 that Stoschek had already considered leaving Berlin about six years earlier when the federal property agency that owns the building demanded a sharp rent rise, and that she had complained the city and federal government were not supporting her work, a dispute former culture senator Klaus Lederer helped settle for the time being. Ocula noted that artists have criticised her over the origins of the family's wealth.
response: Stoschek said Berlin remains important to her and thanked the foundation for its years there; the foundation cited a goal of making the collection available to a broader audience (Ocula, ArtReview, April 2026).
outcome: Berlin space to close end of October 2026; Düsseldorf building due to reopen in 2027.

institution: Julia Stoschek Foundation (Julia Stoschek Collection / JSC Berlin)
headline: Artists press the collector over the Brose family's Nazi-era past
said: The New York Times reported on 29 June 2022 (republished by Artdaily) that artists Leon Kahane, Moshtari Hilal and Sinthujan Varatharajah had called on Julia Stoschek, an heir to the car-parts firm Brose, to deal more openly with her great-grandfather Max Brose's Nazi Party membership and the company's wartime use of forced labour; Kahane said he would not work with her unless she examined the history. Artnet had reported in 2021 that Kahane's 2020 video work put the family's history on show and that critics found a company-commissioned 2008 history insufficiently independent. Stoschek told the Times she welcomed scrutiny but that the collection's wealth was built after the war, that the company paid into the forced-labour compensation fund and that her invitations to Hilal and Varatharajah went unanswered.
where: The New York Times via Artdaily, Artnet
response: Stoschek said the money behind her collection did not come from the Nazi era and that she stands by the 2008 company history (NYT, June 2022). Artnet reported in 2021 that the collection's website carried a Brose statement acknowledging up to 260 forced labourers worked at the company from 1939 to 1945, and that director Robert Schulte pointed to that statement when asked.

headline: KW says it is shedding posts and closing its mediation programme under Senate cuts
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 23 December 2024 that KW director Emma Enderby said the institute was letting positions go, not renewing some contracts and closing a mediation programme after Berlin's government approved around 130 million euros of culture cuts for 2025, and that she called the timing very short notice and very short sighted, with cuts to organisations ranging from about ten to in some cases fifty per cent. In a joint statement with n.b.k., nGbK and Künstlerhaus Bethanien, KW said the planned cuts went well beyond the expected ten per cent, that jobs would be cut or left vacant and programmes cancelled, and warned of a domino effect of lost third-party funding.
where: The Art Newspaper, joint statement on nbk.org
response: Mayor Kai Wegner defended the plan, pointing to a record 40 billion euro budget and blaming the previous administration (The Art Newspaper, 23 December 2024).

headline: n.b.k. and three peers warn the cuts will end their programmatic work
said: In a joint statement published on its website for the 2025 budget, n.b.k. with KW, nGbK and Künstlerhaus Bethanien said the Senate's planned cuts went well beyond the originally expected ten per cent, that budgets were already at their limits because of inflation, energy and rents, and that the larger cuts planned for later years would end their programmatic work if fixed costs stayed the same. ArtDog Istanbul reported on 10 December 2024 that the institutions warned of a domino effect and long-term impoverishment of the city's cultural offer, and that the Berlin Museums Association called the reductions a painful burden especially for smaller institutions.
response: Culture senator Joe Chialo called the cuts very drastic and brutal and pledged to seek alternatives (ArtDog Istanbul, 10 December 2024).

headline: Artists ask why transmediale sacked its artistic director and is not hiring another
said: An open letter dated 1 February 2025 and posted on ArtLeaks, signed by around 38 artists including !Mediengruppe Bitnik, Aram Bartholl, Constant Dullaart and Rosa Menkman, says artistic director Nora O'Murchú was dismissed in summer 2024, that her departure was not transparently communicated and its circumstances remain unresolved, and that instead of the promised call for a new artistic director the festival issued a call for a lead curator on a ten-month contract with the exhibition component removed. The signatories say they fear a powerless curator who gets hired and fired, and ask the leadership to make the basis of its decisions transparent and the advisory board to rethink the festival's structure.
response: No reply from transmediale e.V. or its advisory board found. The letter carries a correction of 2 February 2025 noting that Filippo Gianetta has been managing director since 2020.

headline: New SPK president inherits a 'dysfunctional' foundation and a 2037 Pergamon reopening
said: The Art Newspaper reported on 2 June 2025 that Marion Ackermann took over the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation from Hermann Parzinger after an expert panel had described it in 2020 as dysfunctional and structurally overwhelmed, prompting a January 2025 law that shrinks the board from twenty to nine, moves top staff from civil-servant status to limited-term contracts and removes the Staatliche Museen management layer so individual museums control their own staffing and budgets. The paper wrote that the Pergamon Museum's full reopening is now expected in 2037 at a cost of about 1.5 billion euros, that Berlin Modern's costs have roughly tripled, and that none of Berlin's museums made the 2024 list of the world's hundred most visited.
response: Ackermann called the removal of the Staatliche Museen layer a major relief and said the financial situation remained challenging; funding rises ten per cent to 130 million euros from January 2026 (The Art Newspaper, 2 June 2025).
outcome: Reform law in force from December 2025.

headline: Benin bronzes row: Nigeria hands ownership to the Oba, Germany asks what it returned
